nameStory: The reddening lepiota gets its name from its tendency to develop reddish or pinkish tones when bruised or as it ages. The word 'lepiota' comes from the Greek word for 'scale,' referring to the scaly caps that many mushrooms in this family display, though this species is often smoother than its relatives.
description: The reddening lepiota is a medium to large white mushroom that looks like a classic toadstool with a broad, umbrella-shaped cap and tall stem. It typically grows 4-8 inches across the cap and can reach 6-10 inches tall, making it quite substantial when fully mature. As the common name suggests, it often develops peachy-pink or reddish blushes when handled or cut, especially on the stem and cap edges. This saprobic fungus breaks down dead organic matter like wood chips and sawdust.

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Fresh cuts or bruised areas slowly develop pinkish to reddish stains, especially noticeable on the white stem and cap edges - this color change is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Starts dome-shaped and flattens to umbrella-like with age, typically white to cream colored, smooth or with small scales, feeling dry and slightly fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: White when young, gradually turning pinkish-brown as spores mature, free from the stem (not attached), closely spaced and soft

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thick, white, and sturdy with a prominent ring around the upper portion that can be moved up and down when fresh, hollow or stuffed inside

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Dark brown to nearly black spores when collected on white paper overnight - much darker than many white mushrooms

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, sweet, or slightly almond-like aroma when fresh, sometimes described as reminiscent of anise or licorice

habitat: Look for reddening lepiota in disturbed areas with rich organic matter, especially around wood chips, mulched garden beds, sawdust piles, and decaying stumps. In New England, it's commonly found in suburban areas, parks, and woodland edges where human activity has left behind woody debris. It thrives in well-composted soil and is often seen growing near recently chipped or mulched areas.

seasonality.spring: Early fruiting may begin in late spring after warm rains, particularly in southern New England. Look for small buttons emerging from mulch and wood chip areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for reddening lepiota, especially after summer thunderstorms provide moisture. Mushrooms develop quickly and can appear in flushes throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting into early fall, often producing some of the largest specimens before the first hard frost. Cool, damp September weather is ideal for finding mature mushrooms.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground fruiting in New England winters, though the underground mycelium remains alive in protected organic matter, ready to fruit again next growing season.

funFact: This mushroom can actually move its ring! When fresh, the thick white ring around the stem is loose enough that you can gently slide it up and down like a bracelet - a party trick that works because the ring formed as a protective veil that naturally separated from the stem as the mushroom matured.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other large white mushrooms, especially the destroying angel group, which are deadly poisonous. The key difference is the reddening reaction and dark brown spore print of the reddening lepiota versus the pure white spores and lack of color change in destroying angels. Memory trick: 'Red means read the field guide again, white spores mean take flight!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'lepiota,' this mushroom was moved to the genus Macropsalliota, meaning 'large parasol,' reflecting its substantial size compared to true lepiotas. It was also formerly known by the scientific name Leucoagaricus americanus, so you may see it listed under different names in older field guides.
compareHints: The reddening lepiota is larger and shows more pronounced reddening than its close relative Macropsalliota meleagris. While both have dark spore prints and moveable rings, the reddening lepiota typically grows in wood chip mulch and disturbed soils, whereas other Macropsalliota species may prefer different substrates. The consistent reddening reaction when bruised is more reliable in this species than in its relatives.
